Binary search works by repeatedly dividing the search interval in half.  
At each step it compares the target value with the middle element of the current interval and then **discards the half where the target cannot possibly be** because of the ordering property:

* If the middle element is smaller than the target, the target can only be in the right half (all elements in the left half are ≤ middle < target).  
* If the middle element is larger than the target, the target can only be in the left half (all elements in the right half are ≥ middle > target).

This “discard‑half” reasoning is valid only when the data are **sorted** (either ascending or descending).  
Without sorting, there is no guarantee that elements to one side of the middle are all smaller or larger than the middle, so the algorithm could discard the region containing the target and miss it.
